needs: A laptop with a GPU (or free Colab), public datasets of real and AI-generated images, open-source detectors and watermarking code. No special hardware.
novelty: Your own question: can AI tell AI images from real ones? If yes, flag deepfakes; if not, stamp AI images so a policy can rely on them. The honest answer is 'partly', so pick one side and attack its weak spot. Path A (detect): build a detector using frequency-domain clues (your DSP strength) and test it on images it has never seen, after WhatsApp-style compression and screenshots; the October 2026 'relative patch' detector is a fresh baseline that has not been tested this way. Path B (stamp): measure which watermark designs survive AI re-drawing and the new 'latent frequency masking' attack (which swaps out frequencies inside the AI model's internal code), then try a stamp that survives it; removing a watermark is an image-restoration problem, which is Prof. Giryes's group's core strength. Optional extra from your NVIDIA work: prove that a small image change cannot flip the detector's answer. End with what your numbers mean for an AI-content labeling policy. New support for Path A: an October 2026 study of AI 'dancing' deepfake videos found that generators leave frequency fingerprints that still worked on about 8 in 10 clips from tools and websites the detector had never seen, so the frequency route is promising for video too.
problem: Fake images spread faster than fact-checkers can check them. Today's AI-image detectors work well on the image generators they were trained on but fail on new ones and after an image is compressed or re-shared. Invisible 'stamps' (watermarks such as Google's SynthID) exist, but recent papers show an AI re-drawing of the image can wipe them out, and open-source generators don't stamp anything.
related: Beyond Semantic Features: Pixel-level Mapping for Generalized AI-Generated Image Detection (AAAI 2026)
Exploiting the Final Component of Generator Architectures for AI-Generated Image Detection (2026)
SynthID-Image: Image watermarking at internet scale
Vanishing Watermarks: Diffusion-Based Image Editing Undermines Robust Invisible Watermarking (2026)
Relative Patch Response Learning for Generalizable AI-Generated Image Detection
Exploring Weaknesses of Generative Image Watermarks against Latent Frequency Masking
Stop My Dancing! Understanding, Detecting and Attributing Motion-Aware Deepfake Videos
scope: Two semesters. Semester 1: after a 3-week survey, pick Path A (detect) or Path B (stamp). Gather real photos and AI images from 5–10 generators from public benchmarks (or set up 2–3 open watermarking methods). Run 1–2 existing open detectors or watermarks and measure exactly where they break: unseen generators, WhatsApp-style compression, screenshots, resizing, AI re-drawing. Semester 2: engineer a fix from existing techniques (Path A: frequency-domain features plus compression and screenshot augmentation during training; Path B: the most robust open watermark plus known robustness tricks). Then package it as a usable tool: a web or phone app (or browser extension) where a fact-checker uploads an image and gets a verdict with a confidence level. Test it on real viral images and end with a one-page 'what this means for labeling policy' summary.
title: Telling AI images from real ones: a detector that survives WhatsApp, or a stamp that survives editing

needs: Laptop, public AgentDojo benchmark, open-source CaMeLoT code and a free model checker (nuXmv), plus a small budget for AI-model calls.
novelty: Bring your hardware verification habits to AI: write a few safety rules precisely (like 'never send data to an address the user did not mention'), turn each agent plan or stream of actions into a small state machine, and prove or check the rules automatically. Measuring how many attacks you stop versus how many good tasks you wrongly block, on a public benchmark, is a solid undergrad contribution. Two October 2026 papers make the first weeks easier: one lets an AI draft the safety rules from each app's manual and checks every action with a free logic solver (Z3), and another (SPIDES, open code) shows that labelling data as trusted/untrusted and private/public can block every attack in its test by design.
problem: AI assistants that can send emails, move money or edit files can be tricked by hidden instructions in what they read. Today's protections are mostly 'ask another AI if this looks okay', which can itself be fooled.
related: CaMeLoT: CaMeL orchestrated with Temporal logic for static verification and liveness
Sapien: A Stateful Policy Engine for Autonomous AI Agents
Formal Runtime Verification for Tool-Using LLM Agents: An Offline Same-Benchmark Study on AgentDojo and STAC
Symbolic Constraint Agents: Mining Formal Tool-Call Constraints to Prevent Agent Errors
SPIDES: Information-Flow Control for Browser Agents
scope: Two semesters. Semester 1: set up the public AgentDojo benchmark and the open CaMeLoT / Sapien code. Write 10–20 safety rules for two areas (e.g. email and banking) in a time-aware logic, and check every tool call against them with an existing checker (MonPoly or the Z3 solver). Measure attacks stopped versus good tasks wrongly blocked. Semester 2: turn it into a drop-in safety layer (a Python package or proxy) for an open-source AI assistant, add plan-level checking with the free nuXmv model checker, tune the rules to cut false blocks, and demo it live stopping real prompt-injection attacks. Finish with a short guide on how an organization would deploy it.
title: A safety layer for AI agents that is checked like a chip

needs: A laptop; an existing cellular-link dataset (from your lab or the open OpenMRG Gothenburg dataset), free public GPS-station data, crowdsourced weather-station data, and official records of past floods, storms and heat waves. No sensor building.
novelty: Each of these signals has mostly been used alone, and mostly to measure weather that already happened. Combining several free signals and asking a model to warn hours ahead would be new at undergrad level and builds straight on your CellEnMon work. The hard part, and the interesting one, is 'unprecedented': models learn from the past, so a record-breaking event looks unlike anything in the training data. Treating warnings as 'this is far outside normal' (anomaly detection) instead of only 'this looks like past storms' is a real research question. October 2026 papers give an encouraging answer: free AI weather forecasts (downloadable at no cost) already beat the best physics-based forecast at warning of record-breaking heat, and predict tropical-storm paths better, though they still underestimate peak winds. So a strong baseline is free; your free-signal data could be the local correction on top, for example fixing the too-weak winds or the 'last few hours' that global forecasts miss.
problem: Serious, record-breaking weather (floods, damaging winds, heat waves) kills people most in places with no weather radar and few weather stations, such as much of Africa and rural Asia. But signals that 'feel' the weather already exist almost everywhere: rain weakens the microwave links between cell towers, wind makes those links flicker, moist air delays GPS signals, and cheap home weather stations and even phone battery temperatures track heat.
related: NWS Deploys Improved TACLS to 122 Offices for Earlier Flash Flood Warnings
Fusing geostationary satellite cloud properties with signal attenuation from microwave links for rain detection
Rainfall Sensing via Mobile Communication Signals
Suitable Measures for the Potential Operational Utility of AI NWP Rainfall Forecasts Over Africa
Global inequalities in weather forecasts
Feasibility and limits of commercial microwave links for opportunistic air-temperature monitoring
Probabilistic AI models outperform numerical weather prediction models on record breaking heat extremes
Can AI Forecast the Extremes? Evaluating Probabilistic Weather Models on Tropical Cyclones
scope: Two semesters. Semester 1: pick one region with public data (Israel via CellEnMon links and IMS stations, or the Netherlands / OpenMRG Gothenburg) and list past extreme days: floods, wind storms and heat waves. Gather cellular-link, GPS-delay and crowdsourced weather-station data for those days, and rebuild the known per-hazard signals with existing methods (rain from link signal loss, wind from link flicker, heat from the temperature each link unit logs). Semester 2: combine those signals with a free AI weather forecast as the baseline, using standard ML (gradient boosting or a small network) or an 'unusually extreme' detector, to warn a few hours ahead. Replay past events as if live, measure warning time and false alarms per hazard, and build a simple live warning map or dashboard that a municipality or emergency service could actually use.
title: Early warning for extreme weather from free signals: floods, strong winds and heat waves

needs: Laptop with GPU; the public EasyCom dataset (Meta: smart-glasses microphone array + wide-angle video + labels of who is talking to whom, recorded in a noisy restaurant-like room); open audio-visual speech enhancement code (RAVEN) and pretrained lip models; a webcam and USB microphone (or a phone) for the live demo. For listening tests, volunteers (and ideally hearing-aid users via an audiology clinic, with ethics approval).
novelty: Her own idea (2026-10-31). Not a new algorithm: an end-to-end assistive system built from proven parts. (1) Decide who you're listening to from where your head/camera points (head direction as a simple stand-in for gaze), plus active-speaker detection from lips and faces. (2) Pull that voice out with existing audio-visual speech enhancement (lip-guided, e.g. the open RAVEN code) and/or a beamformer steered toward that person using the glasses' microphones. (3) Mix back a controlled, adjustable amount of the original room sound (residual background), so it sounds natural and you still notice your name or a warning; ideally keep the left/right cues so you can tell where sounds come from. Research shows listeners prefer different amounts of noise removal in different places, so a 'naturalness' slider (or automatic setting per environment) is a useful, testable feature. Fits her Wiener-filter speech enhancement, the hearing-aid paper she starred and her video-processing course.
problem: People with hearing loss struggle most in noisy rooms with several people talking (restaurants, family dinners, classrooms). Difficulty with speech in noise is one of the top reasons people stop wearing their hearing aids. Ordinary hearing aids either amplify everything or reduce steady noise, but they can't tell which of several voices you want. Aggressive noise removal also makes the sound unnatural and tiring, so users often prefer some background to remain.
related: Real-Time System for Audio-Visual Target Speech Enhancement (RAVEN)
The Visual Microphone: Passive Recovery of Sound from Video
EasyCom: An Augmented Reality Dataset to Support Algorithms for Easy Communication in Noisy Environments
Egocentric Auditory Attention Localization in Conversations (CVPR 2023)
Towards Environmental Preference Based Speech Enhancement For Individualised Multi-Modal Hearing Aids (2024)
Visually guided hearing aid (eye-gaze steered beamforming), Boston University / Eriksholm studies
scope: Two semesters. Semester 1 (pipeline on recorded data): set up EasyCom; build the 'who am I listening to?' block (head direction + existing active-speaker detection) and measure how often it picks the right person; run existing enhancement on the chosen speaker (lip-guided network and a steered beamformer, then both combined) and score clarity with standard measures of intelligibility and quality, including hearing-aid-specific ones. Semester 2 (make it usable): add the adjustable natural-background mix and keep left/right cues; make it run in near real time on a laptop/phone with a webcam and microphone; measure delay and lip-sync (too much delay is distracting); run a listening test with volunteers (and, if possible, hearing-aid users) comparing no processing, full noise removal and your natural mix, rating understanding, effort and naturalness. End with a live 'look at someone and hear them' demo.
title: Look-to-listen: camera + microphones that boost the voice you're looking at, and keep the room sounding natural

needs: Public fake-voice datasets (ASVspoof, RealComm benchmark), open-source speech codecs, one GPU. No hardware.
novelty: Most work tests detectors on clean recordings. This project treats the phone call itself as the enemy: model what the microphone, noise removal and network compression do to the voice, train the detector to survive it, and check it separately on older speakers' voices, which current detectors handle worse.
problem: Scammers clone a family member's voice and call older people asking for urgent money. In 2025, people over 60 reported about 7.7 billion dollars in losses to the FBI, and most victims never report at all. Fake-voice detectors exist, but they are trained on clean audio files and get much worse once the voice has passed through a real phone call.
related: RealComm: Benchmarking and Adapting Audio Deepfake Detection over Real Communication Channels
scope: Two semesters. Semester 1: build a 'phone-call simulator' from existing tools (band-limiting to phone quality, open speech codecs, noise suppression, loudspeaker playback) and use it to augment training of an existing open fake-voice detector. Measure the error rate on real call recordings (e.g. the RealComm benchmark) and separately by speaker age. Semester 2: shrink the model so it runs on a phone, build a prototype app that warns the user during a call, test it on newly cloned voices and on older speakers' voices, and write a short practical guide for families and phone companies. Would suit Prof. Giryes's group's strength in reliable neural networks.
title: A fake-voice alarm that works on real phone calls

needs: A laptop and a webcam, free hand-tracking software (MediaPipe), and time to collect videos. No special hardware. A contact in the deaf community or an ISL course would help a lot.
novelty: Very little ISL video data or software exists, so even a working recognizer for a few dozen everyday signs would be new. You could also test a cheap trick from the papers you starred: instead of feeding the whole video to a large AI model, first find the hands and face, then let a small model read only those points over time.
problem: Deaf people in Israel often have no interpreter at a clinic, a bank or a government office. Apps that turn signing into text exist for American and Chinese Sign Language, but almost nothing works for Israeli Sign Language (ISL).
related: SignVLA: Real-Time Sign Language-Guided Robotic Manipulation
Attention-Steered Vision-Language Models for Sign Language Translation
A vision-based sign language recognition and voice conversion system for inclusive communication
scope: Two semesters. Semester 1: collect or gather videos of 50–100 common ISL signs (volunteers or the Israeli deaf community's online dictionaries; get ethics approval if you record people). Track hand and face points with MediaPipe, train an existing small sequence model (GRU or transformer) to recognize single signs, and test it on signers it has never seen. Semester 2: extend to short phrases for one real setting (a clinic or a government office), build a live webcam or phone app that shows the recognized signs as text or speech, run a user test with deaf signers, and report what fails (lighting, fast signing, different hands) and what would be needed for real deployment.
title: A sign-language reader for Israeli Sign Language

needs: A laptop with a GPU (or Colab), public rPPG datasets and open magnification code for semester 1; for semester 2 a hospital partner with ethics approval, or public surgical videos, or your own plant videos. A phone camera for your own tests.
novelty: Your own direction (from your Video Processing course). The goal is not a new algorithm but a useful tool built from existing ones: motion magnification (classic phase-based and open learned magnifiers), optical flow, stabilization and existing camera vital-sign methods, combined with standard ML so the system picks which motion to magnify and turns it into a number a doctor (or farmer) can use. First, check honestly whether magnification helps machines, not just eyes: use it as preprocessing for heart-rate and breathing estimation on public datasets with ground truth (UBFC-rPPG, PURE, rPPG-Toolbox). Then apply the best pipeline to one real problem: neck-vein pressure for heart-failure follow-up (AMPLIFY), Parkinson's tremor (4–6 Hz vs. 8–12 Hz normal tremor), pulsing vessels in surgical video (EndoControlMag), or plant water stress from leaf motion. Known pitfall to engineer around: magnifiers also amplify camera noise (GeoDiffMM, Dec 2025), so frequency-selective filtering and stabilization matter. Likely Giryes fit.
problem: Many warning signs are tiny movements: a pulsing neck vein in heart failure, an invisible Parkinson's tremor, a hidden vessel during surgery, a thirsty plant's drooping leaves. Motion magnification can make them visible, but it was built for human eyes. It also magnifies camera noise and unrelated motion, and doctors still have to judge the video themselves.
related: A novel noninvasive method for remote heart failure monitoring: the AMPLIFY study (npj Digital Medicine 2019)
Seeing the unseen: could Eulerian video magnification aid clinician detection of subclinical Parkinson's tremor? (2020)
EndoControlMag: Robust Endoscopic Vascular Motion Magnification (2025)
GeoDiffMM: Geometry-Guided Conditional Diffusion for Motion Magnification (2025)
Learning-based Video Motion Magnification (Oh et al., ECCV 2018)
DeepMag: Source Specific Motion Magnification Using Gradient Ascent
Enhancing Morpho-Kinematic analysis for Plant Water Stress Classification through Leaf Movements (2025)
scope: Two semesters. Semester 1 (method, public data): weeks 1–3 reproduce classic phase-based and one learned magnifier, and set up rPPG-Toolbox on UBFC-rPPG and PURE; weeks 4–9 measure heart-rate/breathing error with vs. without magnification under added noise and motion; weeks 10–13 build your own frequency-aware or noise-aware magnifier and write a mid-project report. In parallel, find a clinical partner and file for hospital ethics approval (Helsinki committee), which can take months. Semester 2 (real problem): apply the method to one application with real data: neck-vein pressure for heart failure or Parkinson's tremor (partner data), surgical vessels (public videos), or plant water stress (your own plant videos). Turn magnified motion into a number (a measurement or classifier), compare against the reference, and test on people/videos the model never saw. End with a results table, before/after videos, a live demo and a short 'when does magnification help?' guide.
title: Seeing invisible motion: motion magnification + ML that measures, not just shows
